source: original; stimulus is a data table from the U.S. Census Bureau, table HS-42

stimulus.source_note: Data table from U.S. Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract of the United States, table HS-42 (Selected Communications Media, 1920 to 2001).
stimulus.text:
| Year | Share of American households owning a television |
| 1950 | 9.0% |
| 1955 | 64.5% |
| 1960 | 87.1% |

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract, table HS-42. The table gives the share of households owning at least one television set.

stem: Critics such as William H. Whyte worried that the spread of television would deepen conformity in American life. The table best supports that worry in which way?

options.text: Television sets were too costly for most families to buy
options.misconception: The table shows the opposite: by 1960 nearly nine in ten homes owned a set.

options.text: Television reached only a small share of homes by 1960
options.misconception: The table shows 87.1 percent of homes owned a set in 1960, a large share, not a small one.

options.text: Television programs varied widely from one region to another
options.misconception: Background from the books: three national networks fed most sets, so programs were much the same everywhere.

options.text: Nearly nine in ten homes watched the same few national programs

rationales.A: The table shows nearly nine in ten homes owned a set by 1960, so cost had stopped being a barrier.
rationales.B: The table shows 87.1 percent of homes owned a set in 1960, a large share, not a small one.
rationales.C: Background from the books: three national networks fed most sets, so programs were much the same everywhere.
rationales.D: Background from the books: with a set in nearly every home and only three national networks, the same few programs reached almost everyone.
rationales.general:
1. Whyte's worry was that Americans would think and live more alike.
2. The table shows the means for that: a set in nearly nine of ten homes by 1960.
3. Background from the books: only three national networks fed most of those sets, so the same few programs reached almost everyone.
Remember: Conformity grows when one message reaches nearly everyone at once.
